
**Editor Comments**:
        This manuscript presents a flexible framework for estimating thermal tolerance and sensitivity, supported by extensive simulations, empirical examples, and R packages.
        
        I was excited about the manuscript during pre-assessment, particularly because this is an active field with several recent methodological advances. I felt the approach could make a timely and useful contribution.
        
        We received two thoughtful reviews, and I am grateful to both reviewers for their time and expertise. Reviewer 2 is particularly enthusiastic about the methodological rigor and practical utility of the framework, an assessment I largely share. Reviewer 1, while also recognizing these strengths, raises an important concern about novelty, particularly in relation to Bullard et al. (2026).
        
        I think this is the central issue that needs addressing. Both reviewers also offer a number of other useful suggestions for strengthening the manuscript.
        
        I therefore recommend major revision. I see considerable promise in the work, but would like the revision to focus particularly on establishing its novelty. I also intend to seek additional independent reviews of the revised manuscript to help assess this question.
        
The following reviewer comments were taken into consideration during the peer review process.

**Response**: We thank the Editor for recognising the framework's timeliness, utility and rigour. Our central advance is to model $CT_{max}$ and $z$ directly within a single hierarchical dose-response model. These parameters have clear biological meanings, are well established in the TLS literature [Rezende et al. 2014] and support predictions of survival in nature [Rezende et al. 2020]. Upper thermal limits such as $CT_{max}$ also feature widely in comparative and meta-analytic studies [e.g., Sunday et al. 2011; Bennett et al. 2018, 2021; Pottier et al. 2025; Holzmann et al. 2026]. Placing fixed and random effects directly on $CT_{max}$ and $z$ parameters allows comparisons among species, sexes or life stages and decomposition of variation among populations, families or experimental groups, while propagating uncertainty. Reporting uncertainty alongside these estimates also supports more reliable comparative and meta-analytic inference. We derive this parameterisation by building the link between temperature effects on dose-response midpoints and the classical TDT relationship, and provide accessible R packages to implement these joint hierarchical TLS models. All of these points make our work quite novel, and we have tried to do a better job emphasising these points in the Abstract, Introduction and Model specification (Abstract, lines 15–16; Introduction, lines 93–103; Model specification, lines 107–114).

Our revised manuscript also clarifies the relationship to Bullard et al. (2026) (Model specification, lines 107–114; Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 153–158). They identify the log-logistic scale parameter $a$ as median failure time (their Equation 1) and relate its logarithm to temperature (their Figure 2C). However, their increasing-variance prediction workflow estimates these relationships in two stages, fitting curves separately at each temperature before regressing the fitted parameters on temperature (see our detailed response to Reviewer 1 below). Our model estimates temperature effects jointly from the raw data. Flexible asymptotes also distinguish the relative midpoint from absolute 50% survival, for which we derive corrections to $t_{50}$, $CT_{max}$ and $z$. These thresholds coincide in Bullard et al.'s model with asymptotes fixed at 0 and 1 but our case studies show why that restriction does not suit every dataset (Supplement Section 11.5). Finally, our simulations compare bias and interval coverage across experimental designs and changes in steepness and asymptotes, identifying when joint and two-stage estimates agree and when bias or poor coverage emerges. This evaluation of estimator performance provides guidance on modelling and experimental design beyond Bullard et al.'s focus on survival prediction.

**Reviewer 1 Comments to the Author**
 
The manuscript by Noble et al. is a nice methodological contribution that will facilitate implementation of thermal death time / thermal load sensitivity approaches. The R package appears well implemented and thoroughly documented. The documentation is a great resource for the community. My review focuses on my main concern of clarifying the relationship of the model in the manuscript to past models and justifying the differences.

**Response**: We thank Reviewer 1 for their thoughtful review and for recognising our methodological contribution and the value of the R packages. We have revised the manuscript to clarify how the 4PL relates to existing approaches and to compare it with other dose-response models (Model specification, lines 107–140; Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 195–198; Supplement Sections 5 and 11). We favour the log-logistic model because its midpoint links directly to the classical TDT relationship. Other dose-response models can support the same framework, although some require a location adjustment. Our responses below and to Reviewer 2 explain these connections and modelling choices in more detail.

It seems that a similar model (Bullard et al. 2026) was published while the authors were nearing submitting the manuscript. This manuscript cites Bullard et al. (2026) in several places but does not describe the relationship between the models. The models in the research field and their relationship are already difficult to understand and decipher, so I feel that clear describing the relationship of the manuscript's model to Bullard et al. (2026) is essential. The GitHub archive for this manuscript actually contains a solid comparison of the papers that seems to be generated by an AI LLM: https://github.com/daniel1noble/bayesTLS/commit/b27d1490b8bf680c119e3149095fc74242ee4583. I agree with the summary of the comparison:
"The honest framing: **our model is a hierarchical Bayesian generalisation of the log-logistic AFT of @bullard2026, additionally estimating asymptotes and accommodating aggregated proportion/count designs.**"

**Response**: We agree that the relationship should be explicit. With lower and upper asymptotes fixed at 0 and 1, our 4PL gives the log-logistic survival function used by Bullard et al. (2026), with scale $a = 10^{\text{mid}}$ and shape $k/\ln 10$. Our framework extends this description to flexible asymptotes, survival counts, continuous proportions and hierarchical data. We now state this relationship in the paragraph after Equation 3 (Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 153–158; see also Model specification, lines 107–114).

Our main methodological advance is to estimate temperature effects jointly and model $CT_{max}$ and $z$ directly, with fixed and random effects on these parameters. This allows comparisons among species, sexes or life stages and decomposition of variation among families or clones, while propagating uncertainty. Joint estimation differs from Bullard et al.'s increasing-variance prediction workflow, which fits curves separately at each temperature before regressing the fitted parameters on temperature (see the detailed code comparison below). Our simulations evaluate bias and interval coverage of $CT_{max}$ and $z$ across experimental designs and changes in curve shape.

The log-logistic is a convenient starting point because its midpoint links directly to TDT theory, but the framework also applies to other dose-response curves. We now show the corresponding parameterisations for log-normal and Weibull models in the supplement (Supplement Section 5, "Re-parameterisation of alternative dose-response models into TLS models") and implement them in `bayesTLS` through `fit_lognormal()` and `fit_weibull()`.

I briefly describe my understanding of the main differences in the approaches below:
Noble et al. add two more parameters "upper" and "lower" thresholds. The Noble et al. approach fits 4 log-logistic parameters, which are modeled across temperature (introducing more parameters) and are capable of being treated as random effects. Given the relatively small sample sizes of most relevant data to date, the model makes fitting challenging and risks overfitting. The incorporation of thresholds seems to generate some questionable fits in the supplementary examples. The thresholds are not well motivated in the manuscript and it would be helpful to compare the fit of an analogous model without the parameters to justify their inclusion and provide guidance on when thresholds are desirable. The R package is configured to enable fixing the parameters. Since most experiments start with survival of 1 at time 0, the usefulness of the additional parameters seems questionable. The authors mention accommodating “incomplete” data, but I’m not sure how much of an issue such data poses. The survival analysis literature is mature and I believe offers other statistical approaches to left censoring (upper bound) and right censoring (lower bound) data. Overall, the threshold approach should be better justified.

**Response**: We agree that estimating both asymptotes can overfit small datasets, especially when observations do not cover the ends of the response curve. However, it's important to note that these parameters are optional. For example, `fix_asymptotes` in `bayesTLS` allows users to fix either or both, although the default estimates both (Discussion, lines 451–458). Asymptotes of 1 and 0 suit survival assays in which background mortality is negligible and every individual eventually dies, but thi is not a feature of all datasets, as our case studies show (see below).

Free asymptotes can accommodate background mortality or a sublethal response that does not span the full 0–1 range (Ritz et al. 2015).  A short observation window may also leave an asymptote poorly estimated, rather than provide evidence that it differs from 0 or 1.

The model need not include temperature or random effects on every parameter as well, simplifying estimation. Users can share asymptotes and steepness across temperatures and place group effects directly on $CT_{max}$ and $z$. The Discussion already notes that unsupported temperature effects can be omitted (Discussion, lines 449–451) and now explains how to compare fits by WAIC or LOO and when to fix or drop a parameter (Discussion, lines 451–458). We therefore recommend choosing these terms based on the biology, experimental design and predictive checks. Our defaults are there as a first pass to safeguard users.

We have now refitted the zebrafish, cereal aphid and vinegar-fly mortality models with both asymptotes fixed at 0 and 1, which is a two-parameter log-logistic (2PL; Supplement Section 11.5, Table S34). Estimating the asymptotes was clearly better supported for the zebrafish and both sexes of vinegar fly, and favoured, though less clearly, for the cereal aphids. In these survival assays, some individuals died even after the shortest exposures (upper asymptotes of 0.85–0.93 in the flies and aphids) or survived the longest ones (a lower asymptote of 0.20 in normoxic zebrafish). We did not refit the snow gum model because its data already place the upper asymptote below 1, so it is estimated. At the coolest assay temperature (30 °C), its leaves retained on average only 92% of their initial PSII function, and the fitted upper asymptote at the mean assay temperature was 0.95.

Noble et al. include the useful component of modeling uncertainty in total population survival as a binomial distribution, whereas Bullard et al. 2026 just reported the probability. The Bayesian approach in Noble et al. that enables propagating uncertainly is a methodological advance.

**Response**: Thank you. We have made this more explicit. We now state that the joint model makes uncertainty easier to propagate (Model specification, lines 113–114), just before the binomial or beta-binomial likelihood for the counts (Equation 1; Model specification, lines 115–118). We then describe how uncertainty in all estimated quantities is carried through the analysis, with posterior draws propagating it into $CT_{max}$ and $z$ (Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 199–211) and into heat injury and survival probability (Worked examples, lines 318–325).

Noble et al. incorporate repair using a previously published approach (but they don't emphasize that much) whereas Bullard et al. 2026 only describe approaches for accounting for repair.

**Response**: A fair point. We did not focus on repair to avoid overcomplicating the main message of the paper. Arnold et al. (2025) already present the repair model we use, and there are excellent recent papers that model repair and, in some cases, estimate it from data (Buckley et al. 2025; Ørsted et al. 2026; Faber et al. 2026, preprint). Understanding repair is an active research area about which we still know very little. We believe it is better to show how repair can be incorporated in a simple, illustrative form until more is known, which is what we do in the heat-injury predictions (Figure 6; Worked examples, lines 318–323; Supplement Section 15). We note in the Discussion that estimating repair parameters directly from experiments is a major next step (Discussion, lines 464–469).

Noble et al. claim novelty in a "one stage" instead of "two stage" approach, which allows them to propagate uncertainty and changes in shape and thresholds across temperatures. Bullard et al. 2026 is also a one stage approach but they emphasize the fitting to full distributions rather than just using the mean or median survival. I find that characterization of the approach more compelling.

**Response**: Thanks for this comment. Instead of relying on the paper, we went directly to Bullard et al.'s (2026) code. We agree that fitting full failure-time distributions, rather than only mean or median survival, is a real strength of their work, and they do fit single survival regressions of failure time on temperature when choosing among distributions (their S1 and S2 Tables), although with shape held constant. However, we disagree with the description of their increasing-variance prediction workflow, in which shape changes with temperature, as a one-stage analysis. Their implementation fits a log-logistic survival curve separately at each temperature, then regresses the fitted parameters on temperature, as the authors' own code comments state: `#1) First fit log-logistic curves to each tdt curve (each temperature) for the data supplied` and `#2) Then fit a linear model to both log-logistic shape and scale vs temp` ([lines 7–8](https://github.com/gbullard87/Beyond_Mean_TDT_2025/blob/v1.0.0/increasing_var_mod_functions.Rmd#L7-L8)). The function `llogis.mod()` makes these two stages explicit ([increasing_var_mod_functions.Rmd, lines 26–44, release v1.0.0](https://github.com/gbullard87/Beyond_Mean_TDT_2025/blob/v1.0.0/increasing_var_mod_functions.Rmd#L26-L44)). The relevant code is below, with formatting adjusted and some lines omitted:

```r
for (j in unique(TDT.dat$Tref)) {
  mod.j = flexsurvreg(
    Surv(time,event) ~ 1,
    data = TDT.dat[(TDT.dat$Tref==j),], dist = "llogis")
  shape.vec = c(shape.vec,mod.j$coefficients[[1]])
  scale.vec = c(scale.vec,exp(mod.j$coefficients[[2]]))
}

shape.lm = lm(shape.vec ~ unique(TDT.dat$Tref))
scale.lm = lm(log10(scale.vec) ~ unique(TDT.dat$Tref))
```

The subset `TDT.dat$Tref == j` restricts each survival fit to one temperature, and `~ 1` fits it without a temperature predictor. The subsequent `lm()` calls estimate temperature effects from the fitted parameter estimates, one point per temperature. First-stage variances are stored but never used so the regressions are unweighted, and the predictions use only the point estimates of the fitted slopes and intercepts ([lines 68–69](https://github.com/gbullard87/Beyond_Mean_TDT_2025/blob/v1.0.0/increasing_var_mod_functions.Rmd#L68-L69)). This is the implementation used for the fluctuating-temperature predictions, and the main analysis script repeats the function ([lines 1729–1755](https://github.com/gbullard87/Beyond_Mean_TDT_2025/blob/v1.0.0/plosBio_supp_code_2025.Rmd#L1729-L1755)) and calls it for each of those predictions ([lines 2237–2284](https://github.com/gbullard87/Beyond_Mean_TDT_2025/blob/v1.0.0/plosBio_supp_code_2025.Rmd#L2237-L2284)). Fitting full failure-time distributions within each temperature does not make this across-temperature estimation a one-stage analysis. 

Our model jointly estimates temperature effects from the raw response data across temperatures and durations. There is no separate regression step, so uncertainty in every curve parameter carries through to $CT_{max}$ and $z$, which can also take fixed and random effects directly. Bullard et al.'s increasing-variance workflow shares the two-stage structure our simulations evaluate. The two approaches perform similarly when the classical assumptions hold, but two-stage estimates can become biased or poorly calibrated when they do not (Figures 2–4). We have clarified this distinction in the revised manuscript (Model specification, lines 107–114; Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 153–158). We still think our approach is quite novel in that it approaches the problem through a single stage joint estimation approach, propagating uncertainty and direct, hierarchical modelling of $CT_{max}$ and $z$.

Bullard et al. (2026) show empirically that the shape parameter changes with temperature (in violation of the assumptions of previous models). Mentioning this finding in the current manuscript could bolster the motivation for the approach. Noble et al. do include a nice validation of the approach with simulated data. Bullard et al. 2026 discuss the utility of hazard estimates in understanding responses to thermal stress, which could be useful to mention in the current manuscript.

**Response**: A good point! We agree that the shape parameter changing with temperature is important, and supports our justification for placing a temperature effect on k in the 4PL model (which we do by default). Our simulations show that this is important, adding further justification. We have now added this point to the main MS (Model specification, lines 134–138). Regarding hazards, new Supplement Section 5 gives each curve's hazard (Table S12 and Figure S11b) and notes that, with constant $k$, only the Weibull type 1 model has proportional hazards, an assumption Bullard et al. (2026) rejected for *Drosophila* knockdown times.

Overall, the paper would be more useful if it more thoroughly describes the relationship to other modeling approaches and emphasizes areas of novelty. The manuscript and R package is a nice methodological contribution but the methodological upgrades would benefit from more justification.

**Response**: Thanks for your very helpful suggestions. We have tried to better describe the relationship to other modelling approaches, and in particular the work of Bullard et al. 2026 (Introduction, lines 93–103; Model specification, lines 107–140; Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 153–158; Supplement Sections 5 and 11). Please also see our response to Reviewer 2's comments about these points as well. Some are similar.
 
**Reviewer 2 Comments to the Author**
 
General comments
This paper presents a methodologically rigorous and timely contribution to thermal ecology and statistical modeling. The authors successfully address critical limitations in conventional two-stage TDT/TLS analyses by proposing a unified hierarchical four-parameter log-logistic (4PL) model. The framework elegantly avoids problems like failure to propagate uncertainty, mishandling of sparse data where survival doesn't span the full 0–1 range, and pseudoreplication issues inherent to independent temperature-by-temperature analyses. The paper's empirical validation is exceptionally strong. The simulation study systematically compares bias and 95% coverage across 29 scenario-by-design combinations totaling 29,000 simulations, demonstrating that the joint 4PL approach maintains nominal coverage (~0.95) while two-stage methods frequently collapse to values well below this threshold, especially under sparse designs and short exposure windows. The provision of two complementary R packages (bayesTLS and freqTLS) is exemplary and will substantially improve adoption across the biological community.

**Response**: Thank you for these comments. We very much appreciate the enthusiasm for our work and the very constructive feedback. We've tried to address as many points as we can within the space constraints. We believe that the comments from yourself and Reviewer 1 have really helped improve the paper. So, thanks!

Specific Comments
102-115. Model Selection and Justification. While the paper specifies the four-parameter log-logistic function clearly, there is insufficient justification for why this particular functional form was chosen over other flexible sigmoidal alternatives (e.g., Gompertz, Weibull, or other dose-response curves).
I would recommend to add a section comparing the 4PL to 2–3 competing flexible models using information criteria (AIC/BIC) or cross-validation on the empirical datasets. This would strengthen the claim that 4PL is optimal rather than convenient.

**Response**: We thank the reviewer for this comment. It also relates to important points raised by Reviewer 1. The functional form of the dose-response model is not the main contribution of this paper, but they are right to ask about this specifically. To be clear, our key contributions mainly center around: (1) the theoretical connection between a dose-response model's midpoint (or median/location) and the TDT/TLS framework (i.e., making it depend on temperature), (2) re-formalising that model so that CTmax and z become explicit linear predictors and (3) making it much easier to propagate uncertainty into any downstream inferences. As discussed above, Point 2 is particularly important because it means we can model the parameters of interest, CTmax and z, directly - understanding drivers of variance in these estimates, doing explicit variance decomposition and properly doing inference on what matters to biologists. Nonetheless, these connections work for any dose-response curve that has a parameter marking where the curve sits along the time axis (for example the log-logistic, Gompertz or Weibull curves), but it is easiest to explain for the log-logistic. We have now made this clearer in our revised manuscript (Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 195–198; Supplement Section 5).

We focused on using the log-logistic for three reasons, which the manuscript now sets out (Model specification, lines 126–133). First, its midpoint is the time by which half the responding animals have died. That is the LT50, the quantity the TDT theory is typically built on (though we show how to change that). Weibull curves (type 1 has the Gompertz shape on the log-time axis) are lopsided. Their usual location parameter marks where the curve is steepest, after 63% (type 1) or 37% (type 2) of the fall in survival, not 50%. To get the LT50 line from them, the curve must first be rewritten in terms of its midpoint (Supplement Section 5). The log-logistic, like the log-normal, gives it directly. In all cases, however, the midpoint is the 50% point only when the asymptotes sum to 1, as when mortality runs from 0% to 100%. If this isn't true, the 50% point is offset from the midpoint by an amount that depends on the asymptotes and the steepness. If the asymptotes or steepness change with temperature, so does the correction. We give these corrections in the Methods (Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, Equations 4–6, lines 161–185), and they are worked into bayesTLS/freqTLS. Second, there is little evidence that the other curves fit better. In the one published comparison we know of, Bullard et al. (2026) compared the log-logistic with Weibull, log-normal and Gompertz curves on *Drosophila* failure times (11 species). In preliminary analyses the log-logistic fit as well as or better than these curves by AIC in most of the species tested (their S1 and S2 Tables). We have also now added a formal model comparison to each of our case studies that supports this point (see below). Finally, the log-logistic is the most commonly used model in the dose-response literature (e.g., see Ritz 2010 review), which makes it familiar to many readers. We do not claim the log-logistic is optimal, only that it is a sensible default with the most direct link to TDT. Its midpoint is the LT50 when the asymptotes are 0 and 1, and it is the same curve conventional TDT analyses already fit at each temperature, so our model builds directly from existing practice. 

Having said that, we agree a direct comparison on our datasets would help, and we admit that we still do not yet know what model might fit best in all cases. To address this point we have done a few things. First, we have now integrated the log-normal and both Weibull dose-response models into `bayesTLS`, re-parameterising them so that each estimates $CT_{max}$ and $z$ directly. We provide a new section in the supplement (Supplement Section 5) describing this point and making the connections clear. Second, we now do a simple model comparison for each of our case studies, comparing the four curves by approximate leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO) and also reporting WAIC (Supplement Section 11, Tables S29–S33), to which the Discussion now also points (Discussion, lines 452–454). In every case study, the log-logistic was within 1.5 units of expected log predictive density of the best-supported curve, below the roughly 4 units under which models predict about equally well (Sivula et al. 2025), and no single curve was best in every case study. The snow gum comparison is less reliable than the others because of influential observations and sampling problems in the Weibull fits (Supplement Section 11.2).

384-400. Prior Specification and Sensitivity. The paper acknowledges that "Bayesian implementations require priors that are appropriate for the biological system" and that bayesTLS is "designed to make these models more accessible," but prior specifications are relegated to the supplement. The main text lacks discussion of prior sensitivity analysis.

It would be useful to include a brief section (or prominently summarize from the supplement) showing how posterior estimates of thermal sensitivity (z) and CTmax respond to plausible variations in priors. This is essential for readers to understand robustness and reproducibility.

**Response**: Good point. Prior specification was one of the main motivations for also creating the `freqTLS` R package. No priors are needed for these frequentist models. A fit to the same data with `freqTLS` can be compared to `bayesTLS` to ensure that they converge on similar answers. Nonetheless, it is worthwhile exploring prior sensitivity. We have now done that in a new supplement section, which plots the default priors and refits two case studies with weaker and stronger priors (Supplement Section 12, Figure S24 and Table S35), and we summarise the results in the Discussion (Discussion, lines XX–XX).

375-391. Model simplification guidance. The paper states that models "may at times need to be simplified, for example by ignoring temperature-dependent shifts in up, low, or k if they are not well supported by the data," but provides limited concrete guidance on when and how to apply such simplification.
I would recommend to develop a formal model selection approach (e.g., using likelihood ratio tests, AIC, or Bayesian model comparison) with worked examples showing when to retain vs. drop temperature-dependent parameters. Include a decision tree or diagnostic workflow in a figure.

**Response**: Good point. A similar point was raised by Reviewer 1 about model complexity. It is true we didn't help the reader identify when models might be overparameterised even though there are already ample facilities to help identify when simplification is warranted.

To make this clearer, we have now added a few sentences to discuss this point in the Discussion (Discussion, lines 451–458). First, as Reviewer 2 points out, different fits can be directly compared with WAIC or LOO; Supplement Section 11 does this for four dose-response curves in each case study. Supplement Section 11.5 gives a worked example, refitting the zebrafish, cereal aphid and vinegar-fly mortality models with `up` and `low` fixed and comparing each with the default model (Table S34). Fixing them lowered predictive performance in all four comparisons, clearly so in three. Second, simplification can be justified by sampling diagnostics. For example, each parameter should have $\hat{R} < 1.01$ and bulk and tail effective sample sizes above 400, which `diagnose_tdt_fit()` in `bayesTLS` checks. Longer chains with a longer warm-up can help, but if they do not fix these problems, we recommend simplifying the model. We have added greater clarity around this point in our revised manuscript.

282-290. Goodness-of-Fit Metrics. The paper reports realistic R2 values (e.g.,0.695[0.671–0.715] for aphids), much lower than two-stage regressions (0.97–0.996), and correctly notes this reflects fitting raw data. However, the text does not provide alternative fit summaries (e.g., Bayesian R², LOO-CV, or residual diagnostics) to aid practitioners in assessing adequacy.
It might be helpful to expand the goodness-of-fit discussion to include Bayesian R² as computed in brms, leave-one-out cross-validation metrics, and visual residual diagnostics. Show how to interpret these metrics in the context of the 4PL framework.

**Response**: The R² values we report are already the Bayesian R² from `brms` (Worked examples, cereal aphids, lines 332–334; Worked examples, vinegar fly, lines 372–373). We now report sampling diagnostics and a posterior predictive check for every case study (Supplement Sections 6–10), and we compare the log-logistic with other dose-response curves by PSIS-LOO, with Pareto k diagnostics, and WAIC (Supplement Section 11, Tables S29–S33).

331-334. Repair function assumptions. The repair function used in predictions is explicitly acknowledged as "illustrative and not derived empirically." While transparent, this is a substantial assumption for predictions under fluctuating temperature regimes.
It could be insightful to conduct a sensitivity analysis showing how predictions (Figure 6) change across a plausible range of repair rates and kinetics (e.g., from no repair to repair at various rates). Highlight which conclusions are robust to repair assumptions and which are not.

**Response**: Fair point. Please also see our response to Reviewer 1 in regards to this issue. In short, we did not focus on repair to avoid overcomplicating the main message of the paper. Arnold et al. (2025) already present the repair model we use, and there are excellent recent papers that model repair and, in some cases, estimate it from data (Buckley et al. 2025; Ørsted et al. 2026; Faber et al. 2026, preprint). Understanding repair is an active research area about which we still know very little. We believe it is better to show how repair can be incorporated in a simple, illustrative form until more is known, which is what we do in the heat-injury predictions (Figure 6; Worked examples, lines 318–323; Supplement Section 15). Any deeper dive into this is probably another paper as we are space limited. Additionally, we  already capture changes in interpretation when repair processes are accounted for by comparing predictions with and without repair (Worked examples, cereal aphids, lines 335–341; Worked examples, vinegar fly, lines 377–380). The specific values need empirical validation and this is not the purpose of our paper. As such, we have avoided a deep dive into repair.

6. Comparison with Alternative Frameworks. The paper does not discuss or compare the 4PL framework to recent mechanistic thermal tolerance models (e.g., dynamic energy budget models, or more recent machine-learning approaches for dose-response prediction). I’d recommend to add a brief section in the Discussion acknowledging the relationship to (or advantages over) complementary frameworks for thermal tolerance prediction. This would contextualize the 4PL's niche and limitations.

**Response**: Good point. Reviewer 1 also raises this important point in relation to a recent Bullard et al. 2026 paper. We have now added more comparison with Bullard et al. 2026 (Model specification, lines 107–114; Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 153–158), which is a similar idea that clearly came about in parallel to ours, and with other dose-response curves (Supplement Sections 5 and 11). 

We have not added a comparison with dynamic energy budget (DEB) or machine-learning approaches. It is unclear to us which specific studies the reviewer has in mind, and these approaches answer a different question. DEB models predict performance and survival from mechanistic descriptions of energy acquisition and allocation, and machine-learning models predict survival from patterns in data, whereas ours is a statistical framework for estimating thermal tolerance and sensitivity ($CT_{max}$ and $z$), with their uncertainty, from dose-response experiments. Its estimates could, however, serve as inputs to such predictive models. We detail above the distinct differences as we see it and the novelty our approach provides.

Pseudoreplication and Experimental Design Recommendations. While the paper identifies pseudoreplication as a problem with traditional approaches, practical guidance on experimental design to minimize it when using the 4PL is limited. The simulation section tests designs after the fact but does not proactively recommend optimal design. I would recommend to add a section (or expanded Methods discussion) recommending optimal temperature-duration grid designs, replication levels, and handling of nested random effects (e.g., vial-level variation). Use the simulation results to suggest minimal adequate designs for common taxa.

**Response**: We think it is a bit dangerous to "...proactively recommend [a] optimal design". That will depend, to a large extent, on the specific system in question, the expected effect sizes (i.e., magnitude of CTMax and z), and design limitations and characteristics. The point of our simulations were to show that the single stage model provides significant benefits over the two stage model, in terms of correctly estimating z and CTmax, under a variety of different situations.  Some of these were design differences and others were specific to the data. The benefits we show stem from two features of the joint model. First, it estimates the asymptotes and steepness rather than assuming them. Second, it shares information across temperatures and durations, because the curves are linked through shared parameters and their covariance is carried through the fit. This matters most for sparse designs and short exposure windows. More targeted experimental design recommendations will need effect sizes and sample sizes relevant to a given system, as well as the type of question an empiricist wishes to test. In many cases, these simulations will need to be done on a case-by-case basis, which arguably is what we should all be doing before an experiment anyway. We believe our simulations are thorough for comparing the benefits of joint dose-response models to the two-stage approach – as Reviewer 2 points out, 29,000 simulated datasets across 29 scenario-by-design combinations. That's a lot; even for a paper in the statistical literature. We can do more, but it would be good to understand the specific question Reviewer 2 has in mind so we can set up a targeted simulation.

We do agree however that it would be nice to highlight our model's capacity to deal with pseudoreplication. We have now refit our snow gum case study with heat-run and array random effects added to the plant effect, so that the arrays to which light was applied are the replicates, and with zero readings treated as left-censored. Accounting for this non-independence changes the conclusion about post-heat light, which we now make clear in the results and discussion (Worked examples, snow gum, lines 346–353; Figure 5b; Discussion, lines 408–411; Supplement Sections 8.1–8.3).

Computational Requirements and Convergence Diagnostics. The paper provides no discussion of computational demands, convergence diagnostics (R-hat, effective sample size, divergence warnings), or potential convergence challenges users might encounter. I would recommend to include a table summarizing computational time (e.g., for a typical 4-species comparison on standard hardware), guidance on diagnosing non-convergence, and strategies for reparameterization if models fail to converge. This will reduce friction for new users.

**Response**: Good point. Each case study in the supplement now reports how long its main models took to fit, its sampling diagnostics and a posterior predictive check, and Supplement Section 4 gives the hardware (an Apple M1 Max laptop, 10 cores, 32 GB RAM, four chains in parallel). The survival and coma models took 2–15 seconds, the two productivity hurdle models about 2 minutes, and the snow gum model, with three random effects and conservative sampler settings, 53 minutes. `freqTLS` fits the same log-logistic models by maximum likelihood and is faster (Supplement Section 16). The Discussion now also says how to check convergence and what to do when a check fails (Discussion, lines 454–458).

301-314. Case Study Coverage Balance. Three of the four case studies involve relatively well-behaved datasets (aphids, snow gum, vinegar fly). The zebrafish example 10 is noted to have a "sparse design," but only one case study explicitly uses a problematic design. I would recommend to add a brief supplementary case study (or extend zebrafish) demonstrating the 4PL's performance on truly minimal data (e.g., 2 temperatures × 3 durations, N=10 per cell), showing whether the method degrades gracefully or fails. This would clarify practical limits.

**Response**: This is a good idea, but we don't think this is necessary given that we already have fairly extensive simulations. We are not aware of any specific real datasets beyond these ones (and the zebrafish one) that are amenable to such design constraints. Of course, we could add a specific simulated case study but we believe this would be redundant with the simulations, and after all, it is only one realized dataset. Our simulations use 1,000 simulated datasets per scenario-by-design combination (29,000 in total). As such, we've opted to stick with what we have unless there is a specific case study Reviewer 2 has in mind.

394-410. Uncertainty Quantification in Field Predictions. Predictions of survival under field temperature regimes incorporate uncertainty via posterior draws, but the interpretation and use of credible intervals for decision-making (e.g., in conservation) is not discussed.

I would recommend to add guidance on how to interpret wide vs. narrow credible intervals in predictions, and how to translate them into risk assessments or management thresholds (e.g., "if lower 95% CI for survival falls below X%, apply intervention").

**Response**: This is a very good comment. Thanks. We agree this would be helpful. We have now added a sentence to the Discussion on how credible intervals on predicted survival can help inform decisions (Discussion, lines YY–YY).

319-329. Sublethal Endpoints and Hurdle Models. The vinegar fly analysis includes a hurdle model separating reproductive failure from offspring-number changes, but this extension is mentioned only briefly and relegated to the supplement.
I would recommend to elevate one sublethal endpoint (e.g., heat coma or productivity) to the main text with full model specification and biological interpretation. This would demonstrate the framework's flexibility more compellingly.

**Response**: Thanks. Good suggestion. We didn't include it as one of the main examples because we wanted to show diversity of taxa and also a few case studies on how models can be used to calculate heat injury and survival with repair. However, we completely agree that this example would be a very useful addition. (CAN WE ADD A NEW FIGURE HERE and a few sentences?)

Code Availability and Reproducibility. The paper provides R packages but does not explicitly state whether raw data and analysis scripts for all four case studies are publicly available in a repository (GitHub, Zenodo, etc.). I would recommend to add a statement confirming (or clarifying conditions for) open access to scripts, data, and reproducible workflows (e.g., Rmarkdown documents) for each case study. This facilitates replication and community-driven extensions.

**Response**: We apologise that this was not clear. All data and code are public in the GitHub repository (https://github.com/daniel1noble/bayesTLS), which is both the `bayesTLS` package and the research compendium for the paper. The four case-study datasets ship with the package as documented data objects (`aphid_tdt`, `dsuzukii`, `snowgum_psii`, `zebrafish_o2`), with the raw files and temperature traces in `inst/extdata/` and the build scripts in `data-raw/`. The full code for every case study is in `ms/supplement.qmd`, rendered with its code at https://daniel1noble.github.io/bayesTLS/, and `ms/ms.qmd` builds the manuscript, taking the case-study figures and numbers from outputs that `ms/supplement.qmd` saves. The simulation is run by `scripts/simulations/run_simulations.R`. Stored model fits and simulation outputs are on OSF (https://osf.io/c6dxy) and can be downloaded with `make data` on terminal or bash, or just downloaded directly. We have expanded the Data and code availability statement in the manuscript to name the case-study datasets, where their raw files, temperature traces and build scripts are, the file with the full case-study analyses, the simulation script and the OSF archive (Data and code availability, lines 498–508).

Minor Comments
233-25. Figure 4 presents complex multi-panel comparisons that would benefit from a more detailed caption explaining the distinction between "sparse" and "full" designs and the biological implications of bias at different replication levels.

**Response**: Great point. We have added two supplement figures that draw the simulated designs (Figures S30 and S32, Supplement Section 13.6), and the Figure 4 caption, which already defined the full and sparse grids, now points to them. We also rewrote the Simulations text on where two-stage estimates are most biased. Specifically, on sparse grids and at the two shortest exposure caps. Even with the $t$-correction, two-stage coverage of $z$ falls sharply at those two time caps, whereas on sparse grids it stays close to nominal but with much wider intervals than the joint model's. This corrects our earlier statement that two-stage coverage collapsed as grids became sparser (Simulations, lines 291–298).

The use of "relative" vs. "absolute" thresholds for CTmax is introduced conceptually but could be clarified earlier with a simple worked example in the Introduction.

**Response**: Thank you. We considered adding a worked example to the Introduction but decided against it, because it would make the Introduction harder to follow and the distinction is already set out in the main text. We have, however, clarified that relative and absolute thresholds coincide whenever the asymptotes sum to 1 (Figure 1 caption; Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 153–158; Deriving key thermal load sensitivity parameters, lines 164–167), and new Supplement Figure S11 marks both thresholds on example curves.

Summary Assessment
This is a substantive and well-executed paper that makes important methodological contributions to thermal ecology. The authors demonstrate rigor, acknowledge limitations candidly, and provide practical tools. The recommendations above are aimed at enhancing clarity, robustness, guidance, and practical utility rather than addressing fundamental flaws. Implementation of even a subset of these suggestions would further elevate the paper's impact and accessibility to practitioners.

**Response**: We would like to sincerely thank Reviewer 2 for their extremely thoughtful and constructive review. We are very happy they find the work rigorous, and that they think it will make an important methodological contribution to the field. We have made every attempt to try and take on board as many of the suggestions as possible. At times, some of these points were not easily accommodated within the word limits of the paper, and so, apologies if not all points were adequately addressed.
